title: The Last Honours for a Deceased
sentences: 'Well, this is taking a long time, I tell you!
I've been standing here in the cold for a good half hour.
Do you think I mean to freeze to death?
Come on, move along, mate!
You've seen worse in your life.'
But just then the door of the house of death was opened, and a curious forward press arose among the onlookers.
The narrow alley, with its dim light, was wholly white from fallen snow;
only the ink-black hearse and the curious ones at the house of death stood out like a sombre patch of mourning against the untouched white.
A fine east wind swept along the weathered, sagging façades of the poor houses,
lifting snow from gutters and window-sills and letting it fall in soft clumps onto the street.
The alley was soundless; the clamour of voices was muffled by the snow.
And slowly, shuffling backward, two men in black came out of the door,
holding a coffin at the foot end; two others held it at the head.
'Damn it, the old Willems made that coffin himself from
cigar boxes!
What a colour!
Red as his drowned face!'
The bare, grey-wood coffin had been set with its foot end on the rim of the hearse, an old,
faded black carriage, without ornament, poor, worn, ever keeping a smell of death in its dark depth.
The two rows of onlookers who had stood from the hearse to the door closed in behind the coffin,
around the carriage, rising on their toes, pushing one another, curious, anxious not to miss a movement of the black men.
Two of the bearers had walked round behind the carriage and took hold of the coffin from the far side, through the hearse.
'Come, forward!
One, two — heave!'
With a thud the coffin was pulled entirely inside.
People talked all around.
The old Willems had surely never thought of this — four crows to carry him off in his equipage.
Boys!
you'd die for pleasure;
your whole life trailing an old vegetable cart and after your death being taken away in a gala carriage!
Pity you could only take such a ride once. Yet people still whispered; women,
with arms folded under their breasts, kept somewhat back; labourers and street boys pressed forward.
The mystery of death held them.
The four bearers, skilled at their work, able at a glance to tell how heavy a corpse weighed,
reared in a poor man's smell of death, did their labour without speaking, understanding one another at a sign.
The carelessness with which they went about their work filled the onlookers with a kind of admiration; and the black men,
sure of their importance in the eyes of the crowd, did not even deign a glance, proceeding mechanically.
But when one of them caught his finger under the coffin and brought it to his mouth in pain, loud laughter burst out.
Faith, old Wil-
lems still bites!
A wicked rascal, I say!
Why didn't such an ugly crow keep his filthy fingers at home?
And when the man turned round furiously, the shouting and laughter grew louder still.
'Yes, old fellow, it's a poisonous bite!
Take care — you'll die of it; your turn will come too, I tell you!'
The driver on the high box, above two lean black horses, had turned impatiently.
Were they dreaming at their work?
He had no intention of freezing for their pleasure — none at all!
The wretched coffin now stood upright, between four black wooden posts, with a faded cloth over it.
The crowd slowly drew back; its curiosity was satisfied and the impression of the first moment had faded.
It had made the coffin its own, and it seemed as though the drowned face of old Willems were visible through the wooden boards;
yes, they saw him lying there, eyes turned upward, hands folded on his lean belly.
For years he had daily slouched through the streets with his grey beard and tangled hair.
He had lain so often, in his threadbare clothes, drunk in the gutter,
that many thought he was snoring in a stupor again.
The thought of his corpse no longer inspired horror;
no one gave it a moment's thought and had come to see everything for strangeness and novelty, without thinking of the dead body.
Several pushed into the house of death, whose door still stood open.
The room the dead man had lived in was a hovel: four bare walls,
smoke-stained and damp, speaking of filthy poverty, holding a moist, foul air.
The few pieces of furniture stood and lay in great disorder;
two chairs had been placed in the middle of the room a little apart from each other; they had borne the coffin.
People even crowded into this room, at first stick-
ing their heads through the doorway, slowly pressing one another forward,
finally abandoning all restraint, sniffing about corners and cupboards.
Remarks were whispered; people pointed at certain objects to confirm some earlier claim;
some women examined old rags from a cupboard, felt the little stove and opened its door to look inside.
But one of the black men came angrily running into the room, grumbling that he was hindered in the quick dispatch of his work,
and drove the curious mob out, slamming the door shut behind them.
At last the hearse drove away.
The four black men fell in behind in a row, not marching in step,
arms hanging, stamping their feet to warm them, now and then breaking into a little trot
to catch up again with the hearse, which drove much too fast.
And without any seriousness or ceremony it went, swinging heavily in the old harness,
round the corner of the alley, followed by the indifference of the curious.
The gathered crowd gradually dispersed;
a small group remained a moment before the house talking, ever dwindling, melting into the surrounding cottages.
A young workman, leaving with several others, called out to an old woman,
tall in stature and with a face fallen through grief, the wife of an innkeeper:
'Hey, mother, that's bankruptcy for the man, isn't it?
You'll miss a good customer like old Willems, won't you!'
But the woman answered nothing, and went on, looking silently before her, more bent than before.
And the alley returned to its former stillness,
losing the curious life of a moment first in the middle, spreading its solitude toward both ends; some spar-
rows flew down from the roofs to the place where the snow had been trampled hard before the house of death;
the noise of hoarse voices from a small tavern died away in the snow-silence.
And swiftly the hearse went on, shaking frightfully to and fro, to reach the cemetery.
The four men who followed were jostled in the busy streets by passers-by,
had now to dodge a carriage, then skirt great heaps of snow, continually breaking their row and resuming their talk in fragments.
Hardly anyone noticed the hearse, or if one chanced to see it,
one immediately turned one's head away, startled for a moment at having forgotten that wretched unpleasantness.
The main streets and the Noordeinde were driven through quickly, without a sound, the rolling of wheels in the snow muffled,
as though one glided over a soft carpet in a vast hall,
surrounded only by the talk of passers-by, whose voices rang fresh and clear in the fine winter air.
Thus one came at last to the Scheveningen road, which in a gentle,
dead silence, with deep perspective, bored like a tube toward the horizon.
At the toll there was no one to be seen; a fishwife
approaching at some distance with a handcart formed a small black dot.
The trees on either side of the road, their branches thickened by snow, stretched cramp-like, white arms above the hearse.
On the left gleamed the garden of the Grand Duchess of Saxe-Weimar, on the right the Boschjes, with their low wood,
the feet of the trees surrounded by a scribble and stir of white veins,
fragments of a forest, high on the hills, petrified in its white cold, eternally frozen and snow-covered.
In the distance, where the branches of the trees facing each other met, the belly
of a gigantic monster seemed to stretch out, covered with white sand, resting on a thousand green legs on both sides.
And faster the hearse hurried on, as through a colonnade of the finest marble.
Suddenly it turned right, onto the Cemetery Lane, which in its white stiffness ran to a point against the cemetery.
Now it was as though one had entered one of the great passages that in the high,
underground North, belonging to the realm of the Ice King, lead to his crystalline palace.
The white house at the cemetery closed off the perspective.
The black blot of the hearse moved on, wagging and shaking, like a drunken beast; the four black men followed in a row,
one behind another, to use as much as possible the places trodden flat by the hearse and those before them.
The snow lay deep; now and then a thick piece fell from the trees
with the soft rustle of satin cloth; above the lane hung a grey sky, heavy with snow.
Thus the cemetery was reached, the men panting, the horses steaming under their faded black cloths.
The white house was driven past and then a turn was made to the left.
In the depth of the cemetery, behind a hedge of sugar-white shrubs, a pit had been dug.
And the stone graves lifted the snow cover everywhere with soft curves, here and there raising a dark pillar from it.
The hearse stopped, and the gravediggers were called.
Two big fellows, sturdily built, with high-red faces, appeared in thick duffel coats.
The cloth was torn off the coffin with a jerk;
one gravedigger took it at the foot end and with a strong pull drew it onto the rim of the hearse;
the other took it at the head, and both carried it like a large bundle to the grave.
'Remember, we've got another at eleven,
mind!'
called one of the black men.
'Right!
right!'
answered from the distance one of the gravediggers.
The four bearers climbed into the black carriage; one pulled his legs in after him.
At a trot the carriage drove away,
gradually making its black dot on the white snow smaller and smaller until it finally vanished altogether.
The two gravediggers remained behind with the coffin by the open pit.
It was deathly still all around; only the earth falling on the coffin
for a moment made the life of a hailstorm clattering against window-panes.
And it began to snow, inaudibly soft, in large flakes.
